ops.text:
The binrun-shim fragment's "bash, not sh" comment overclaims, and every repo taking the cc-guides render inherits the claim verbatim.

Source: plugin/guides/sh/binrun-shim.sh:14-16, rendered into plugins/slop-cop/scripts/install-binary.sh:16 and plugins/codex/scripts/install-binary.sh:16 in this repo, and into plugin/scripts/install-binary.sh in every downstream consumer. Verbatim:

    # bash, not sh: this runs once per hook invocation, and an endpoint-security agent
    # that deep-inspects /bin/sh as a living-off-the-land interpreter can put seconds on
    # every exec of it. The body is POSIX either way.

Two problems, neither of which is a reason to revert the change:

1. It reads as a shell swap, and it isn't one. On macOS /bin/sh IS bash invoked in POSIX-compat mode, so moving the shebang from /bin/sh to /bin/bash does not change interpreters. What it changes is which binary PATH gets executed, and therefore which path an endpoint-security agent's rules match on. That path-based-inspection framing is plausible and may well justify the change; the current wording just isn't saying it.

2. "can put seconds on every exec of it" is an unmeasured figure presented as fact. Either measure it (a before/after exec-time comparison under whatever EDR motivated the change) and cite the number, or soften to something that doesn't quantify — e.g. "an endpoint-security agent whose rules match on /bin/sh can add per-exec inspection latency that /bin/bash avoids".

Asking for a measurement or softer wording, NOT a revert: the shebang change itself is defensible and should stay.

How this surfaced: writing the cc-present v0.33.0 CHANGELOG (released, tag v0.33.0). The install-binary.sh shebang change rode along in the release range via cc-guides 0.1.53, I changelogged it as user-visible, and lifted this comment's rationale into the entry — so the overclaim is now shipped in cc-present's changelog too. Not re-tagging over one clause; fixing the fragment is the real remedy, since per-repo fixes would be chasing copies of a single source.
